subject: physics
question_text: Show that C_P − C_V = R for an ideal gas.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya IPE Study Material for Jr. Students 2026-27 edition, physics volume, Chapter 12 (Thermodynamics) Short Answer Question 3 (printed p.127). Only the question was taken; the answer, its steps and its mark split are original work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. The four-way mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked: for one mole at constant volume ΔQ = C_V ΔT = ΔU since no work is done; at constant pressure ΔQ = C_P ΔT = ΔU + PΔV; from PV = RT at constant P, PΔV = RΔT; substituting gives C_P ΔT = C_V ΔT + RΔT, so C_P − C_V = R, where C_P and C_V are the MOLAR specific heats of one mole of an ideal gas.

steps.label: At constant volume
lines: Consider ONE MOLE of an ideal gas.
At constant volume no work is done,
so all the heat raises the internal
steps.margin_note: Say ONE MOLE and NO WORK AT CONSTANT VOLUME before writing the relation.
steps.why: C_V is DEFINED using this exact condition — no work — so the derivation must start here, not with the general first law.
common_mistakes: Starting from ΔQ = ΔU + ΔW directly without first setting ΔW = 0 for the constant-volume case.
Forgetting to say ONE MOLE — the whole derivation works in molar quantities.
steps.memory_tip: No volume change, no work — all the heat becomes internal energy, ΔQ = ΔU.

steps.label: At constant pressure
lines: At constant pressure the gas also
expands and does work PΔV, so more
heat is needed for the same rise
steps.margin_note: Include the PΔV term — this is the extra term that constant-volume heating does not have.
steps.why: This is the same first law applied to the OTHER condition, and the PΔV term is exactly the extra heat that makes C_P bigger than C_V.
common_mistakes: Dropping the PΔV term and writing ΔQ = ΔU only — that is the constant-volume case, not this one.
Writing W without its constant-pressure form PΔV — at constant pressure, work equals P times the change in volume.
steps.memory_tip: At constant pressure, work PΔV rides along with ΔU — that is the extra heat C_P needs.

steps.label: PΔV in terms of R
lines: For one mole, PV = RT. At constant
steps.margin_note: This step turns the work term PΔV into RΔT — the key substitution.
steps.why: PV = RT is the equation of state for one mole; holding P fixed and taking the small change gives exactly the PΔV the previous step needs.
common_mistakes: Using PV = nRT with n left in, instead of setting n = 1 for one mole.
Forgetting that P is held CONSTANT here — only V and T change.
steps.memory_tip: One mole, constant P: PΔV turns straight into RΔT.

lines: C_P and C_V here are the MOLAR

steps.margin_note: State clearly that C_P and C_V here are the MOLAR specific heats, not per unit mass.
steps.why: This relation holds only for the molar specific heats; the per-unit-mass forms satisfy a different relation, c_P − c_V = R/M, so the word MOLAR is not optional.
common_mistakes: Writing C_P − C_V = R without saying these are molar specific heats — the same-looking per-mass forms c_P, c_V do NOT satisfy this relation.
Stopping at C_P ΔT = C_V ΔT + RΔT without dividing by ΔT to reach the final relation.
steps.memory_tip: Divide the constant-pressure equation by ΔT and the ΔT cancels, leaving C_P − C_V = R for one mole.

insider_note: C_P − C_V = R holds for the MOLAR specific heats only — for the per-unit-mass forms c_P and c_V it becomes c_P − c_V = R/M.
